primitives.name: Upset Frequency
primitives.verbatim_quote: Characterize parity via the variance σ of season-end winning fractions and predictability via the measured upset frequency q (fraction of games where the team with the worse record on game day wins), and build a model linking the two.
primitives.assumptions: All teams start equally; fixed q; random pairing; favorite defined by current record; ties as half-win.
primitives.breakdown_regime: q < 0.5 implies predictable outcomes; q → 0.5 implies maximal randomness.

layer2.mapping: q serves as a proxy for league predictability; used in GSE's season-level calibration of moneyline probabilities.
layer2.telemetry: Observed fraction of games won by worse-recorded teams.

primitives.name: Winning Fraction Variance
primitives.verbatim_quote: Characterize parity via the variance σ of season-end winning fractions and predictability via the measured upset frequency q (fraction of games where the team with the worse record on game day wins), and build a model linking the two.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: σ = standard deviation of winning fraction x; dimensionless.
primitives.assumptions: Teams begin equal; variance arises from stochastic process; season length finite.
primitives.breakdown_regime: σ → 0 implies perfect parity; σ → 1 implies extreme imbalance.

layer2.mapping: σ quantifies dispersion in team performance; informs GSE's confidence bounds on win probabilities.
layer2.telemetry: Variance of final season winning fractions across teams.

primitives.name: Monte Carlo Simulation Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model Mock-league Monte Carlo: teams start equal, are paired at random, play a fixed (sport-specific) number of games; the team with the better record is the favorite; the underdog wins with fixed upset probability q < 1/2.
primitives.assumptions: Equal starting teams; fixed q; random pairing; deterministic game outcomes.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Model valid for large N; finite season effects captured via interpolation.

layer2.mapping: Simulated season outcomes mirror real-world parity dynamics; enables GSE to simulate competitive landscapes.
layer2.telemetry: Distribution of simulated season-end winning fractions.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that competitive balance in sports can be quantified using two complementary metrics: the upset frequency q and the variance σ of winning fractions. The former measures unpredictability, while the latter captures dispersion in team performance. These are linked through a nonlinear model where σ decreases with increasing q and season length. This relationship allows for season-level priors in GSE’s moneyline calibration. The model assumes equal starting conditions, fixed q, and random pairing, which simplifies but may miss structural factors like salary caps or scheduling changes. The derived kernel maps q into a predictive index for GSE, while σ provides uncertainty bounds. The Monte Carlo simulation validates this framework by generating synthetic seasons that match empirical distributions. However, the model lacks explicit team strength and ignores game context such as location and margin, limiting its fidelity in high-stakes scenarios.
